Dissuade

/dih-SWAYD/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Dissuade means to persuade someone not to do something

Dissuade means to persuade someone not to do something. Her counselor tried to dissuade her from dropping the chemistry course just one week before the final.

Worked Example

A storm warning flashed across the news just as Lena grabbed her keys for a midnight drive up the mountain. Her parents laid out the forecast, the icy switchbacks, and the closed ranger stations one by one. In the end they dissuaded her from going, and she left safely at dawn instead.

The parents did not forbid the trip or take the keys; they used reasons and evidence to convince Lena not to go, which is exactly what dissuade means.

How Dissuade Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

deter

deter: to discourage someone from acting

discourage

discourage: to weaken someone's will to do something

talk out of

talk out of: to convince someone not to do something

Antonyms

encourage

encourage: to urge someone on toward an action

urge

urge: to push someone strongly to act

How Strong Is It? — discourage → dissuade → prevent

discourage vs. dissuade

discourage vs. dissuade: Discourage is milder than dissuade; you can discourage someone with a frown, but dissuading them means actually convincing them not to act.

prevent vs. dissuade

prevent vs. dissuade: Prevent is stronger than dissuade because it stops the action entirely, while a dissuaded person still freely chooses not to act.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: against, away

Root — suade

Root — suade: from Latin suadere, to urge or advise

Put it together

Put it together: Dissuade joins dis-, meaning against, with the Latin suadere, to urge or advise, so it literally means to urge against. The same root gives us persuade, to urge someone toward something, and suave, which originally meant agreeable.

Use the root in a new word: persuasion

Use the root in a new word: persuasion: Her gentle persuasion convinced the committee to fund the new library wing.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral to formal

Dissuade almost always takes 'from': you dissuade someone from doing something, usually through reasons and argument rather than force. It is the direct opposite of persuade, which shares the same Latin root; persuade urges someone toward an action, while dissuade urges them away from it.
